items.stem: In a sigmoid growth curve, why does the population level off?
options: All individuals stop reproducing
The population has no limiting factors
Mutations stop
Limiting factors such as food and space reduce the birth rate or increase the death rate
items.answer: Limiting factors such as food and space reduce the birth rate or increase the death rate
items.markingKey: D. Births ≈ deaths at carrying capacity.

items.stem: "Populations always grow until every individual has died of starvation." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Most populations stabilise around carrying capacity because birth and death rates balance.
items.markingKey: Most populations stabilise around carrying capacity because birth and death rates balance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a population can briefly overshoot the carrying capacity.
items.answer: Resources take time to run out; individuals born when food was plentiful continue to consume until shortage increases deaths, then the population falls back.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Resources take time to run out; individuals born when food was plentiful continue to consume until shortage increases deaths, then the population falls back. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to Reindeer on St Matthew Island (1944–1966), explain how it illustrates overshoot and crash.
items.answer: 29 reindeer introduced to a predator-free island grew to about 6000 by 1963, ate the lichen, and crashed to 42 after a hard winter. It shows what can happen when a population exceeds carrying capacity with no predators.
items.markingKey: Context (29 reindeer introduced to a predator-free island grew to about 6000 by 1963, ate the lichen, and crashed to 42 after a hard winter.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It shows what can happen when a population exceeds carrying capacity with no predators. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to overshoot and crash.

items.stem:
Felix counted duckweed fronds in a beaker of pond water every 4 days (three beakers).

Time / days | Number of fronds: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
4 | 38 | 37 | 37
8 | 119 | 113 | 151
12 | 246 | 241 | 254
16 | 342 | 338 | 347
20 | 363 | 391 | 378

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean number of fronds at 8 days, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 151 (trial 3 at 8 days); mean = 116.0
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (151) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 116.0.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Culling deer is the best way to protect woodland from overgrazing."
items.answer: Culling is often necessary where natural predators are absent, but long-term solutions may include predator reintroduction.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: quickly reduces numbers below carrying capacity; protects young trees and biodiversity. Arguments against: ethical objections to killing animals; reintroducing predators (e.g. wolves, lynx) or fencing could be more natural. Supported judgement: Culling is often necessary where natural predators are absent, but long-term solutions may include predator reintroduction.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "carrying capacity"?
options: Linked rises and falls in predator and prey populations, with predator peaks lagging behind prey peaks
An S-shaped curve with lag, exponential and plateau (stationary) phases
A diagram showing the energy flowing through each trophic level per unit area per year; always pyramid-shaped
The maximum population size that an environment can support indefinitely
items.answer: The maximum population size that an environment can support indefinitely
items.markingKey: D. "carrying capacity" is the maximum population size that an environment can support indefinitely.

items.stem: Distinguish between logistic (sigmoid) growth and exponential growth.
items.answer: Exponential growth has no limits and accelerates (J-curve); logistic growth slows as limiting factors act and levels off at the carrying capacity (S-curve).
items.markingKey: Exponential growth has no limits and accelerates (J-curve); logistic growth slows as limiting factors act and levels off at the carrying capacity (S-curve). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why introducing rabbits to Australia led to a population explosion.
items.answer: There were few predators, little competition, plenty of food and suitable habitat, so the limiting factors on growth were removed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: There were few predators, little competition, plenty of food and suitable habitat, so the limiting factors on growth were removed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Kenji is investigating how the initial concentration of glucose affects the maximum population of yeast in a culture. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If the glucose concentration is higher, then the maximum population will be higher, because more food raises the carrying capacity until another factor such as ethanol becomes limiting.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If the glucose concentration is higher, then the maximum population will be higher, because more food raises the carrying capacity until another factor such as ethanol becomes limiting.

items.stem: Sketch and describe a sigmoid population growth curve for yeast in a flask, explaining each phase in terms of limiting factors.
items.answer: Lag phase: few cells, adjusting, little division. Exponential (log) phase: plenty of glucose, cells divide rapidly, numbers double regularly. Stationary phase: glucose runs low, ethanol and waste build up, births = deaths – carrying capacity. Death phase (in a closed flask): food exhausted, toxins high, deaths exceed births.
items.markingKey: Lag phase: few cells, adjusting, little division. Exponential (log) phase: plenty of glucose, cells divide rapidly, numbers double regularly. Stationary phase: glucose runs low, ethanol and waste build up, births = deaths – carrying capacity. Death phase (in a closed flask): food exhausted, toxins high, deaths exceed births.

items.stem: Which process releases most of the energy “lost” between trophic levels?
options: Excretion of oxygen
Respiration, as heat
Decomposition only
Photosynthesis
items.answer: Respiration, as heat
items.markingKey: B. Also undigested material and uneaten parts.

items.stem: A student claims: "Energy is lost from the ecosystem when it is lost from a trophic level." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Energy lost from a level is transferred to the surroundings as heat or to decomposers; it is not destroyed.
items.markingKey: Energy lost from a level is transferred to the surroundings as heat or to decomposers; it is not destroyed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between gross primary productivity and net primary productivity.
items.answer: GPP is the total energy captured by producers in photosynthesis; NPP is what is left after producers’ own respiration and is available to consumers.
items.markingKey: GPP is the total energy captured by producers in photosynthesis; NPP is what is left after producers’ own respiration and is available to consumers. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A cow eats grass containing 5000 kJ. It loses 2000 kJ in faeces and 1200 kJ in respiration. Calculate the energy available for growth and the percentage efficiency of conversion to biomass.

Elena measured the energy stored per square metre at each trophic level of a lake ecosystem in three different years.

Trophic level | Energy stored / kJ/m² per year: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
1 | 27827.8 | 28051.3 | 29024.7
2 | 2769.9 | 2951.3 | 2793.1
3 | 291.3 | 283.6 | 276.6
4 | 27.8 | 28.1 | 29.4
5 | 2.9 | 2.8 | 2.8

Calculate the mean energy stored when the trophic level was 1.
items.answer: 28301.27 kJ/m² per year
items.markingKey: M1 (27827.8 + 28051.3 + 29024.7) ÷ 3; A1 28301.27 kJ/m² per year (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Diego plans to investigate how the mass of food eaten by mealworms affects the increase in their biomass. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: number and starting mass of mealworms (20); temperature (25 °C); moisture (same slice of carrot each week); container size
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: number and starting mass of mealworms (20) – larger mealworms grow differently; temperature (25 °C) – affects respiration and growth; moisture (same slice of carrot each week) – water affects survival; container size – crowding affects growth. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Use energy-flow ideas to explain why a field of wheat can feed more people if they eat the bread than if the wheat is fed to cattle and they eat the beef. Include a calculation with 10% efficiency per step.
items.answer: If wheat stores 100 000 kJ: eating wheat directly gives ~10 000 kJ to humans (10% of it assimilated, simplified); feeding cattle first gives ~10 000 kJ to cattle and only ~1000 kJ to humans. The extra trophic level loses ~90% through respiration (heat), movement, undigested material; so about 10× more people can be fed from crops.
items.markingKey: If wheat stores 100 000 kJ: eating wheat directly gives ~10 000 kJ to humans (10% of it assimilated, simplified); feeding cattle first gives ~10 000 kJ to cattle and only ~1000 kJ to humans. The extra trophic level loses ~90% through respiration (heat), movement, undigested material; so about 10× more people can be fed from crops.

items.stem: "Insect farming should replace beef as a major protein source." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Insects are a much more efficient protein source and could reduce environmental impact, though acceptance will take time.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: insects convert feed to biomass much more efficiently (cold-blooded); much less land, water and greenhouse gas. Arguments against: cultural reluctance to eat insects; allergy risks; welfare and scale-up questions. Supported judgement: Insects are a much more efficient protein source and could reduce environmental impact, though acceptance will take time. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A diagram showing the energy flowing through each trophic level per unit area per year; always pyramid-shaped"?
options: carbon sink
carrying capacity
pyramid of energy
nitrogen fixation
items.answer: pyramid of energy
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of pyramid of energy.

items.stem: Briefly explain why there are rarely more than five trophic levels in a food chain.
items.answer: Only about 10% of energy is passed on each step, so after four or five transfers too little energy remains to support a population.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Only about 10% of energy is passed on each step, so after four or five transfers too little energy remains to support a population. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Herbivores convert all the plant material they eat into their own biomass." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Much is egested undigested and much energy is used in respiration; only a small fraction becomes herbivore biomass.
items.markingKey: Much is egested undigested and much energy is used in respiration; only a small fraction becomes herbivore biomass. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Silver Springs, Florida (Odum, 1957) shows quantifying energy flow.
items.answer: Howard Odum measured energy flow through every trophic level of a spring ecosystem, finding that each level received only about 10–20% of the previous one’s energy. It was one of the first complete energy budgets of an ecosystem and established the energy pyramid idea.
items.markingKey: Context (Howard Odum measured energy flow through every trophic level of a spring ecosystem, finding that each level received only about 10–20% of the previous one’s energy.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It was one of the first complete energy budgets of an ecosystem and established the energy pyramid idea. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to quantifying energy flow.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the mass of food eaten by mealworms affects the increase in their biomass, state the dependent variable and describe how Nia should measure it.
items.answer: increase in total mass of 20 mealworms over 2 weeks
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: increase in total mass of 20 mealworms over 2 weeks.

items.stem: Kenji investigated how the mass of food eaten by mealworms affects the increase in their biomass. The method had this weakness: the frass (faeces) was weighed with the leftover bran. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: sieve the bran to separate frass before weighing
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: sieve the bran to separate frass before weighing

items.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
options: Decomposition
Photosynthesis
Respiration
Combustion
items.answer: Photosynthesis
items.markingKey: B. Carbon is fixed into glucose.

items.stem: "Carbon atoms are created by plants." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Carbon atoms are not created or destroyed; they are recycled between compounds and reservoirs.
items.markingKey: Carbon atoms are not created or destroyed; they are recycled between compounds and reservoirs. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between respiration and photosynthesis in the carbon cycle.
items.answer: Respiration releases CO₂ to the atmosphere from all organisms; photosynthesis removes CO₂ and fixes it into organic compounds in producers.
items.markingKey: Respiration releases CO₂ to the atmosphere from all organisms; photosynthesis removes CO₂ and fixes it into organic compounds in producers. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Ana measured the CO₂ concentration in the air inside a closed greenhouse at different times of day (three days).

Time of day / h | CO₂ concentration / ppm: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
4 | 593 | 556 | 581
8 | 539 | 528 | 539
12 | 425 | 426 | 451
16 | 400 | 375 | 402
20 | 438 | 451 | 442

State the time of day at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 4 h; range = 37 ppm; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 4 h; 1 range = max − min = 593 − 556 = 37 ppm; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: With reference to The Keeling Curve (Mauna Loa, 1958–present), explain how it illustrates long-term monitoring.
items.answer: Charles Keeling began measuring atmospheric CO₂ on Mauna Loa in Hawaii; the record shows a yearly zig-zag and a rise from about 315 ppm to over 420 ppm. It is the clearest direct evidence of rising atmospheric CO₂ from human activities.
items.markingKey: Context (Charles Keeling began measuring atmospheric CO₂ on Mauna Loa in Hawaii; the record shows a yearly zig-zag and a rise from about 315 ppm to over 420 ppm.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It is the clearest direct evidence of rising atmospheric CO₂ from human activities. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to long-term monitoring.

items.stem:
A class is planning an investigation into how light intensity affects the uptake of carbon dioxide by pondweed, measured with hydrogencarbonate indicator.
(a) Write a focused research question. [1]
(b) Explain how the independent variable will be changed, giving a suitable range. [1]
(c) Describe how the dependent variable will be measured and how many repeats are needed. [2]
(d) Explain how volume of indicator (10 cm³) will be controlled and why. [1]
(e) Identify one safety or ethical consideration. [1]
items.answer: (a) How does distance of the lamp from the tube affect colour change of hydrogencarbonate indicator after 1 hour? (b) distance of the lamp from the tube (10, 20, 30, 40 cm) – at least five values across a sensible range. (c) colour change of hydrogencarbonate indicator after 1 hour, measured as absorbance in a colorimeter; at least three repeats and a mean. (d) volume of indicator (10 cm³) – affects colour change. (e) keep water away from the lamp and mains sockets.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 names IV and DV. (b) 1 method of changing the IV with ≥5 values. (c) 1 measurement method with instrument/units; 1 ≥3 repeats and mean. (d) 1 how and why volume of indicator (10 cm³) is controlled (affects colour change). (e) 1 relevant point, e.g. keep water away from the lamp and mains sockets.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how light intensity affects the uptake of carbon dioxide by pondweed, measured with hydrogencarbonate indicator. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Put 10 cm³ of red hydrogencarbonate indicator (equilibrated with air) into tubes; add 5 cm³ of pondweed and seal; place tubes at each distance from an LED lamp behind a water heat shield; include control tubes; after 1 hour measure absorbance at 550 nm; repeat three times; plot absorbance against light intensity (1/d²).
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (keep water away from the lamp and mains sockets). Model: Put 10 cm³ of red hydrogencarbonate indicator (equilibrated with air) into tubes; add 5 cm³ of pondweed and seal; place tubes at each distance from an LED lamp behind a water heat shield; include control tubes; after 1 hour measure absorbance at 550 nm; repeat three times; plot absorbance against light intensity (1/d²).

items.stem: "Carbon capture and storage at power stations is the best way to tackle rising CO₂." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: CCS can help for hard-to-decarbonise industries, but cutting emissions with renewables is cheaper and more certain.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: captures up to 90% of CO₂ from large sources; allows use of existing infrastructure. Arguments against: expensive and energy-intensive; risk of leaks; storage sites limited; may delay switching to renewables. Supported judgement: CCS can help for hard-to-decarbonise industries, but cutting emissions with renewables is cheaper and more certain. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "decomposition".
items.answer: The breakdown of dead organic matter by bacteria and fungi, releasing CO₂ by respiration
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the breakdown of dead organic matter by bacteria and fungi, releasing CO₂ by respiration. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how marine organisms with shells take part in the long-term carbon cycle.
items.answer: They use carbon to make calcium carbonate shells; after death shells form sediments that become limestone, locking carbon away for millions of years.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They use carbon to make calcium carbonate shells; after death shells form sediments that become limestone, locking carbon away for millions of years. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between respiration and photosynthesis in the carbon cycle.
items.answer: Respiration releases CO₂ to the atmosphere from all organisms; photosynthesis removes CO₂ and fixes it into organic compounds in producers.
items.markingKey: Respiration releases CO₂ to the atmosphere from all organisms; photosynthesis removes CO₂ and fixes it into organic compounds in producers. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Atmospheric CO₂ at Mauna Loa was 370 ppm in 2000 and 424 ppm in 2024. Calculate the mean rate of increase in ppm per year.
items.answer: 2.25 ppm per year

items.stem: A student claims: "Planting trees permanently removes carbon dioxide." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Trees store carbon while alive, but release it when they die and decompose or burn unless the wood is preserved.
items.markingKey: Trees store carbon while alive, but release it when they die and decompose or burn unless the wood is preserved. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Draw (describe) the carbon cycle, naming four processes that move carbon, and explain how human activities have changed it.
items.answer: Photosynthesis (atmosphere → plants), feeding (plants → animals), respiration (organisms → atmosphere), decomposition (dead matter → decomposers → atmosphere), combustion (fossil fuels/biomass → atmosphere), fossilisation and ocean dissolution. Humans: burning fossil fuels and deforestation add CO₂ faster than sinks absorb; less photosynthesis; CO₂ rose from 280 to over 420 ppm, enhancing the greenhouse effect and acidifying oceans.
items.markingKey: Photosynthesis (atmosphere → plants), feeding (plants → animals), respiration (organisms → atmosphere), decomposition (dead matter → decomposers → atmosphere), combustion (fossil fuels/biomass → atmosphere), fossilisation and ocean dissolution. Humans: burning fossil fuels and deforestation add CO₂ faster than sinks absorb; less photosynthesis; CO₂ rose from 280 to over 420 ppm, enhancing the greenhouse effect and acidifying oceans.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "precipitation"?
options: Water falling from clouds as rain, snow or hail
A reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases, e.g. oceans, forests, peat
Linked rises and falls in predator and prey populations, with predator peaks lagging behind prey peaks
Growth in which the population increases by the same proportion in each time interval, giving a J-shaped curve
items.answer: Water falling from clouds as rain, snow or hail
items.markingKey: A. "precipitation" is water falling from clouds as rain, snow or hail.

items.stem: Kenji writes: "The water cycle only involves evaporation and rain." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It also includes transpiration, condensation, infiltration, run-off, groundwater flow and storage in ice and organisms.
items.markingKey: It also includes transpiration, condensation, infiltration, run-off, groundwater flow and storage in ice and organisms. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between nitrification and nitrogen fixation.
items.answer: Nitrogen fixation turns N₂ gas into ammonia/ammonium; nitrification turns ammonium into nitrites then nitrates.
items.markingKey: Nitrogen fixation turns N₂ gas into ammonia/ammonium; nitrification turns ammonium into nitrites then nitrates. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Jonas measured the nitrate concentration of a stream at different distances downstream from a field fertilised in spring (three samples each).

Distance downstream / m | Nitrate concentration / mg/dm³: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 37.0 | 36.4 | 37.8
100 | 25.5 | 26.3 | 25.8
200 | 18.5 | 19.8 | 19.7
400 | 11.2 | 10.9 | 10.7
800 | 5.6 | 5.7 | 5.8

Calculate the mean nitrate concentration when the distance downstream was 100 m.
items.answer: 25.87 mg/dm³
items.markingKey: M1 (25.5 + 26.3 + 25.8) ÷ 3; A1 25.87 mg/dm³ (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Amara plans to investigate how the mass of nitrate fertiliser added affects the growth of duckweed. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: starting number of fronds (10); light intensity and duration; temperature; volume of water (200 cm³)
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: starting number of fronds (10) – more plants give more growth; light intensity and duration – needed for photosynthesis; temperature – affects growth rate; volume of water (200 cm³) – affects nutrient concentration. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Ingrid investigated how the mass of nitrate fertiliser added affects the growth of duckweed. The method had this weakness: tap water was used, which already contains nitrate. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: use distilled water with a nitrate-free nutrient solution
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: use distilled water with a nitrate-free nutrient solution

items.stem: Define the term "transpiration".
items.answer: The loss of water vapour from leaves, part of the water cycle
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the loss of water vapour from leaves, part of the water cycle. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain how nitrogen in a dead leaf becomes available to another plant.
items.answer: Decomposers break down proteins into ammonium compounds; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrites and then nitrates; plant roots absorb nitrates by active transport.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Decomposers break down proteins into ammonium compounds; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrites and then nitrates; plant roots absorb nitrates by active transport. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to The Haber process and the nitrogen cycle, explain how it illustrates human impact on nutrient cycles.
items.answer: Industrial fixation of nitrogen into ammonia now roughly doubles the natural rate of nitrogen fixation; about half the world’s food depends on it. Fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication and nitrous oxide emissions, showing a trade-off between food and environment.
items.markingKey: Context (Industrial fixation of nitrogen into ammonia now roughly doubles the natural rate of nitrogen fixation; about half the world’s food depends on it.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication and nitrous oxide emissions, showing a trade-off between food and environment. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to human impact on nutrient cycles.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the mass of nitrate fertiliser added affects the growth of duckweed, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: volume of water (200 cm³).
items.answer: affects nutrient concentration
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (volume of water (200 cm³)) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: affects nutrient concentration. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: "Organic farming without artificial fertilisers can feed the world." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Organic methods can reduce pollution, but feeding everyone would probably also need efficient use of some artificial fertiliser and less food waste.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: healthier soils, less pollution and eutrophication; legumes and manure recycle nitrogen. Arguments against: yields are typically 20–25% lower; would need more land, possibly causing deforestation. Supported judgement: Organic methods can reduce pollution, but feeding everyone would probably also need efficient use of some artificial fertiliser and less food waste. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ecological efficiency"?
options: The percentage of energy at one trophic level that is transferred to the next
The breakdown of dead organic matter by bacteria and fungi, releasing CO₂ by respiration
The dry mass of living material in organisms
The position of an organism in a food chain (producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer …)
items.answer: The percentage of energy at one trophic level that is transferred to the next
items.markingKey: A. "ecological efficiency" is the percentage of energy at one trophic level that is transferred to the next.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The long-term capture and storage of carbon dioxide"?
options: limiting factor
pyramid of biomass
exponential growth
carbon sequestration
items.answer: carbon sequestration
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of carbon sequestration.

items.stem: What is happening in the lag phase of a bacterial growth curve?
items.answer: Cells are adjusting and making enzymes before dividing rapidly
items.markingKey: Cells are adjusting and making enzymes before dividing rapidly. Growth is slow.

items.stem: Explain why deforestation can reduce local rainfall.
items.answer: Trees transpire large volumes of water vapour that forms clouds; fewer trees means less water vapour and less precipitation downwind.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Trees transpire large volumes of water vapour that forms clouds; fewer trees means less water vapour and less precipitation downwind. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why measuring biomass destroys the organisms and how ecologists reduce this problem.
items.answer: Organisms must be dried to constant mass; ecologists take small samples and use estimates from known wet-to-dry ratios.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Organisms must be dried to constant mass; ecologists take small samples and use estimates from known wet-to-dry ratios. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why atmospheric CO₂ concentration rises in winter and falls in summer in the Northern Hemisphere.
items.answer: In summer, photosynthesis by plants exceeds respiration, removing CO₂; in winter many plants lose leaves and photosynthesis falls while respiration and decomposition continue.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In summer, photosynthesis by plants exceeds respiration, removing CO₂; in winter many plants lose leaves and photosynthesis falls while respiration and decomposition continue. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between exponential growth and logistic (sigmoid) growth.
items.answer: Exponential growth has no limits and accelerates (J-curve); logistic growth slows as limiting factors act and levels off at the carrying capacity (S-curve).
items.markingKey: Exponential growth has no limits and accelerates (J-curve); logistic growth slows as limiting factors act and levels off at the carrying capacity (S-curve). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between denitrifying bacteria and nitrifying bacteria.
items.answer: Nitrifying bacteria (aerobic) make nitrates available to plants; denitrifying bacteria (anaerobic) turn nitrates back into N₂ gas, reducing soil fertility.
items.markingKey: Nitrifying bacteria (aerobic) make nitrates available to plants; denitrifying bacteria (anaerobic) turn nitrates back into N₂ gas, reducing soil fertility. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a pyramid of numbers and a pyramid of biomass.
items.answer: A pyramid of numbers counts individuals at each level and can be any shape (one tree supports many insects); a pyramid of biomass shows the dry mass at each level and is usually pyramid-shaped.
items.markingKey: A pyramid of numbers counts individuals at each level and can be any shape (one tree supports many insects); a pyramid of biomass shows the dry mass at each level and is usually pyramid-shaped. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Tomás measured the CO₂ concentration in the air inside a closed greenhouse at different times of day (three days).

Time of day / h | CO₂ concentration / ppm: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
4 | 548 | 545 | 543
8 | 499 | 505 | 492
12 | 431 | 436 | 407
16 | 374 | 367 | 367
20 | 420 | 423 | 412

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: CO₂ concentration is highest before dawn, falls through the morning to a minimum in the afternoon and rises again in the evening. At night only respiration occurs, adding CO₂; in daylight photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so plants take CO₂ from the air.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: CO₂ concentration is highest before dawn, falls through the morning to a minimum in the afternoon and rises again in the evening.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: At night only respiration occurs, adding CO₂; in daylight photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so plants take CO₂ from the air.

items.stem: A population of duckweed plants increased from 450 to 750 in 10 weeks. Calculate the mean rate of population growth.
items.answer: 30 per week
items.markingKey: M1 (750 − 450) ÷ 10; A1 30 individuals per week.

items.stem: Briefly describe The Haber process and the nitrogen cycle and explain what it reveals about human impact on nutrient cycles.
items.answer: Industrial fixation of nitrogen into ammonia now roughly doubles the natural rate of nitrogen fixation; about half the world’s food depends on it. Fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication and nitrous oxide emissions, showing a trade-off between food and environment.
items.markingKey: Context (Industrial fixation of nitrogen into ammonia now roughly doubles the natural rate of nitrogen fixation; about half the world’s food depends on it.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication and nitrous oxide emissions, showing a trade-off between food and environment. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to human impact on nutrient cycles.

items.stem: Producers in a grassland store 50000 kJ/m² per year, and primary consumers store 5000 kJ/m² per year. Calculate the ecological efficiency of the transfer.
Atmospheric CO₂ at Mauna Loa was 317 ppm in 1960 and 414 ppm in 2020. Calculate the mean rate of increase in ppm per year.
items.answer: 1.62 ppm per year

items.answer: maximum yeast cell count per mm³ (haemocytometer) over 5 days
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: maximum yeast cell count per mm³ (haemocytometer) over 5 days.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the mass of food eaten by mealworms affects the increase in their biomass. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Weigh 20 mealworms and place in a container with a known mass of bran; keep at 25 °C in the dark; after 2 weeks reweigh mealworms and remaining bran (sieve out frass); calculate mass eaten and gain in mass; calculate % conversion; repeat with three containers per mass.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (wash hands after handling animals and bran; treat animals humanely and return them to the culture). Model: Weigh 20 mealworms and place in a container with a known mass of bran; keep at 25 °C in the dark; after 2 weeks reweigh mealworms and remaining bran (sieve out frass); calculate mass eaten and gain in mass; calculate % conversion; repeat with three containers per mass.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how light intensity affects the uptake of carbon dioxide by pondweed, measured with hydrogencarbonate indicator. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): keep water away from the lamp and mains sockets. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. keep water away from the lamp and mains sockets); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the initial concentration of glucose affects the maximum population of yeast in a culture. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Prepare 50 cm³ of each glucose solution with the same nutrients; add 1 cm³ of yeast suspension; incubate at 25 °C; each day shake and take a 0.1 cm³ sample; count cells with a haemocytometer under a microscope; repeat with three flasks per concentration; plot growth curves and find the maximum.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (use aseptic technique; dispose of cultures after disinfection; handle glass slides carefully). Model: Prepare 50 cm³ of each glucose solution with the same nutrients; add 1 cm³ of yeast suspension; incubate at 25 °C; each day shake and take a 0.1 cm³ sample; count cells with a haemocytometer under a microscope; repeat with three flasks per concentration; plot growth curves and find the maximum.

items.stem: Explain the roles of four different types of bacteria in the nitrogen cycle and suggest how waterlogged soil affects plant growth.
items.answer: Nitrogen-fixing (free-living and in legume nodules): N₂ → ammonium. Decomposers (putrefying): proteins/urea → ammonium. Nitrifying: ammonium → nitrites → nitrates (aerobic). Denitrifying: nitrates → N₂ (anaerobic). Waterlogged soil: little oxygen – nitrifiers inhibited, denitrifiers thrive – nitrates fall – plants become nitrogen deficient (yellow leaves, poor growth); roots also lack oxygen for respiration.
items.markingKey: Nitrogen-fixing (free-living and in legume nodules): N₂ → ammonium. Decomposers (putrefying): proteins/urea → ammonium. Nitrifying: ammonium → nitrites → nitrates (aerobic). Denitrifying: nitrates → N₂ (anaerobic). Waterlogged soil: little oxygen – nitrifiers inhibited, denitrifiers thrive – nitrates fall – plants become nitrogen deficient (yellow leaves, poor growth); roots also lack oxygen for respiration.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "ecological efficiency".
items.answer: The percentage of energy at one trophic level that is transferred to the next
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the percentage of energy at one trophic level that is transferred to the next. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "carbon sink"?
options: A reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases, e.g. oceans, forests, peat
The rate at which producers store energy as biomass after their own respiration
Swellings on the roots of legumes containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria
A factor in short supply that restricts population growth, such as food, space, light or nesting sites
items.answer: A reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases, e.g. oceans, forests, peat
items.markingKey: A. "carbon sink" is a reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases, e.g. oceans, forests, peat.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "density-dependent factor".
items.answer: A factor whose effect increases as population density increases, e.g. competition, disease
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a factor whose effect increases as population density increases, e.g. competition, disease. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why farmers grow clover or beans in crop rotation.
items.answer: Bacteria in root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium compounds; when the crop is ploughed in, the soil gains nitrates for the next crop, so less fertiliser is needed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Bacteria in root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen into ammonium compounds; when the crop is ploughed in, the soil gains nitrates for the next crop, so less fertiliser is needed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a carbon source and a carbon sink.
items.answer: A carbon source releases more carbon than it absorbs (e.g. burning forests, power stations); a sink absorbs more than it releases (e.g. growing forests, oceans).
items.markingKey: A carbon source releases more carbon than it absorbs (e.g. burning forests, power stations); a sink absorbs more than it releases (e.g. growing forests, oceans). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between logistic (sigmoid) growth and exponential growth.
items.answer: Exponential growth has no limits and accelerates (J-curve); logistic growth slows as limiting factors act and levels off at the carrying capacity (S-curve).
items.markingKey: Exponential growth has no limits and accelerates (J-curve); logistic growth slows as limiting factors act and levels off at the carrying capacity (S-curve). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between nitrifying bacteria and denitrifying bacteria.
items.answer: Nitrifying bacteria (aerobic) make nitrates available to plants; denitrifying bacteria (anaerobic) turn nitrates back into N₂ gas, reducing soil fertility.
items.markingKey: Nitrifying bacteria (aerobic) make nitrates available to plants; denitrifying bacteria (anaerobic) turn nitrates back into N₂ gas, reducing soil fertility. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why mammals and birds have lower ecological efficiency than reptiles.
items.answer: They use much energy in respiration to maintain a constant body temperature, so less is converted to biomass for the next level.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They use much energy in respiration to maintain a constant body temperature, so less is converted to biomass for the next level. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using Reindeer on St Matthew Island (1944–1966) as an example, explain overshoot and crash.
items.answer: 29 reindeer introduced to a predator-free island grew to about 6000 by 1963, ate the lichen, and crashed to 42 after a hard winter. It shows what can happen when a population exceeds carrying capacity with no predators.
items.markingKey: Context (29 reindeer introduced to a predator-free island grew to about 6000 by 1963, ate the lichen, and crashed to 42 after a hard winter.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It shows what can happen when a population exceeds carrying capacity with no predators. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to overshoot and crash.

items.stem: Lars is investigating how the mass of nitrate fertiliser added affects the growth of duckweed. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If more nitrate is added, then the duckweed will grow more fronds, because nitrates are needed to make amino acids and proteins for new cells, up to a point where another factor limits growth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If more nitrate is added, then the duckweed will grow more fronds, because nitrates are needed to make amino acids and proteins for new cells, up to a point where another factor limits growth.

items.stem: With reference to Silver Springs, Florida (Odum, 1957), explain how it illustrates quantifying energy flow.
items.answer: Howard Odum measured energy flow through every trophic level of a spring ecosystem, finding that each level received only about 10–20% of the previous one’s energy. It was one of the first complete energy budgets of an ecosystem and established the energy pyramid idea.
items.markingKey: Context (Howard Odum measured energy flow through every trophic level of a spring ecosystem, finding that each level received only about 10–20% of the previous one’s energy.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It was one of the first complete energy budgets of an ecosystem and established the energy pyramid idea. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to quantifying energy flow.

Leila measured the nitrate concentration of a stream at different distances downstream from a field fertilised in spring (three samples each).

200 | 18.0 | 18.4 | 18.7
400 | 10.7 | 10.8 | 14.6

items.answer: Anomaly: 14.6 mg/dm³ (trial 3 at 400 m); mean = 10.75 mg/dm³

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Insect farming should replace beef as a major protein source."
items.answer: Insects are a much more efficient protein source and could reduce environmental impact, though acceptance will take time.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: insects convert feed to biomass much more efficiently (cold-blooded); much less land, water and greenhouse gas. Arguments against: cultural reluctance to eat insects; allergy risks; welfare and scale-up questions. Supported judgement: Insects are a much more efficient protein source and could reduce environmental impact, though acceptance will take time.

items.stem: Elena plans an investigation into how light intensity affects the uptake of carbon dioxide by pondweed, measured with hydrogencarbonate indicator. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (distance of the lamp from the tube (10, 20, 30, 40 cm)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Culling deer is the best way to protect woodland from overgrazing."
items.answer: Culling is often necessary where natural predators are absent, but long-term solutions may include predator reintroduction.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: quickly reduces numbers below carrying capacity; protects young trees and biodiversity. Arguments against: ethical objections to killing animals; reintroducing predators (e.g. wolves, lynx) or fencing could be more natural. Supported judgement: Culling is often necessary where natural predators are absent, but long-term solutions may include predator reintroduction. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.
